'''''Panicum repens''''' is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] known by many common names, including '''torpedo grass''', '''creeping panic''', '''panic rampant''', '''couch panicum''', '''wainaku grass''', '''quack grass''', '''dog-tooth grass''', and '''bullet grass'''. Its exact native range is obscure. Sources suggest that the grass is native to "Africa and/or Asia",<ref name=fla>[http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/node/308 ''Panicum repens''.] University of Florida Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants.</ref> "Europe or Australia",<ref>[http://www.sms.si.edu/irlspec/panicum_repens.htm ''Panicum repens''.] Smithsonian Marine Station at Fort Pierce.</ref> "Eurasia",<ref name=ms>Byrd, J. D. and V. Maddox. [http://www.gri.msstate.edu/ipams/FactSheets/Torpedo_grass.pdf Torpedograss (''Panicum repens'' L.)] Mississippi State University Extension.</ref> "Australia",<ref name=texas>[https://aquaplant.tamu.edu/plant-identification/alphabetical-index/torpedograss/ Torpedograss.] Texas A&M AgriLife Extension.</ref> "Europe, Asia, and Africa",<ref name=hoss>Hossain, M. A., et al. (1999). [https://www.jstor.org/pss/4046129 Effect of burial depth on emergence of ''Panicum repens''.] ''Weed Science'' 47(6) 651-56.</ref> or other specific regions, including the [[Mediterranean]], and [[Argentina]].<ref name=feis>Stone, Katharine R. 2011. [http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/graminoid/panrep/all.html ''Panicum repens''.] In: Fire Effects Information System, [Online]. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory.</ref> It is present in many places as an [[introduced species]] and often a [[noxious weed]]. It has been called "one of the world's worst weeds."<ref name=ms/>

==Overview==
This perennial grass spreads via its large, branching [[rhizome]]s, which are thick and pointed. The pointed shape of the rhizome tip gives the plant the name torpedograss. The rhizomes creep along the ground or float in water, forming floating mats. They can reach a length of {{convert|6|m|abbr=on}} and a soil depth of {{convert|7|m|abbr=on}}, and they can form a mat {{convert|15|cm|abbr=on}} thick. The spreading rhizomes sprout repeatedly to form colonies of stems.<ref name=feis/> The stems are {{convert|20|to|90|cm|abbr=on}} tall,<ref name=gm>[http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Panicum_repens&type=treatment ''Panicum repens''.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304053623/http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Panicum_repens&type=treatment |date=2016-03-04 }} Grass Manual Treatment.</ref> sometimes reaching {{convert|1|m|abbr=on}}. They grow erect or bend down. The leaves are stiff and straight, linear in shape, and flat or folded. They are sometimes white in color and waxy in texture. The [[inflorescence]] is a loose [[panicle]] of branches bearing small spikelets {{convert|2|to|3|mm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=feis/><ref name=gm/>

==Habitat==
This grass grows throughout the world in tropical and subtropical areas. It was introduced to the United States in seed for [[forage]] grasses and probably in [[ballast]] water from ships. It was also imported by the [[United States Department of Agriculture]] to grow as a forage grass for cattle. It was deliberately planted throughout South [[Florida]] and it easily escaped cultivation,<ref name=feis/> eventually becoming "one of the most serious weeds in Florida," spreading to more than 70% of the waterways in the state.<ref name=fla/> In [[Lake Okeechobee]], it has invaded more than 16,000 acres of [[marsh]].<ref name=feis/> It displaces native plants,<ref name=smith>Smith, B., et al. (1993). [http://www.apms.org/japm/vol31/v31p199.pdf Factors influencing the efficacy of glyphosate on torpedograss (''Panicum repens'' L.).] ''J Aquat Plant Manage'' 31 199–202.</ref> growing colonially in thick, [[Monotypic habitat|monotypic]] stands.<ref name=ms/> Dense mats or stands of the grass cause [[Hypoxia (environmental)|hypoxia]] in the water.<ref name=feis/> Torpedograss management in flood-control systems costs an estimated US$2 million per year.<ref name=ms/>

The plant is established in sandy coastal habitat on the United States' [[Gulf Coast]], such as beaches and [[dune]]s, from Florida to [[Texas]], where it occurs with beach plants such as [[Batis maritima|turtleweed]] (''Batis maritima''), [[Distichlis spicata|saltgrass]] (''Distichlis spicata''), [[Fimbristylis spadicea|marsh fimbry]] (''Fimbristylis spadicea''), [[Hydrocotyle bonariensis|largeleaf pennywort]] (''Hydrocotyle bonariensis''), and [[Salicornia bigelovii|dwarf saltwort]] (''Salicornia bigelovii''). It grows on many [[barrier island]]s. It grows in many types of [[wetland]] habitat, in and out of the water. It grows in freshwater marshes, [[salt marsh]]es, [[mud flat]]s, wet [[prairie]]s, [[tide pool]]s, [[bog]]s, and lakesides. It also invades drier habitat, such as coastal pine forests and [[Florida scrub|white sand scrub]]. It easily moves into disturbed and cultivated areas such as [[ditch]]es and canals.<ref name=feis/> It is a nuisance in [[sod]] production.<ref name=fla/> In other areas, it can be found in [[Sod|turf]] and [[orchards]].<ref name=hoss/> In the Florida turfgrass industry, it is the second-worst weed known.<ref name=steph>Stephenson, D. O., et al. (2006). [https://www.jstor.org/pss/4495688 Control of torpedograss (''Panicum repens'') with trifloxysulfuron-sodium in bermudagrass (''Cynodon dactylon'' x ''Cynodon transvaalensis'') turf.] ''Weed Technology'' 20(2) 351-55.</ref> The grass can grow in a variety of habitats, but it does not tolerate cold and it is rarely found above subtropical latitudes or at altitude.<ref name=feis/>

==Propagation==
The grass spreads primarily via its rhizome. It has been noted to grow {{convert|1.3|cm|abbr=on}} in length per day. The stems and rhizomes also produce [[Tiller (botany)|tillers]]. The rhizome can endure drying and flooding. Dry or wet conditions may reduce the number of shoots produced by the rhizome, but they do not kill it. The rhizome can disperse when parts of it break off and drop onto the substrate elsewhere, anchoring and putting up new shoots. The plant survives and sprouts after [[herbicide]] application, grazing, cutting, plowing or disking, and burning. The grass rarely reproduces by seed.<ref name=feis/> It has been noted to reproduce by seed in Portugal,<ref name=steph/> but does not do so in the United States,<ref name=busey>Busey, P. (2003). [https://www.jstor.org/pss/3989463 Reduction of torpedograss (''Panicum repens'') canopy and rhizomes by quinclorac split applications.] ''Weed Technology'' 17(1) 190-94.</ref> and it was described as "incapable of fruiting" in Japan. [[Seeds]] are sometimes observed but they are apparently rarely viable, with many studies describing zero [[germination]].<ref name=feis/>

The grass has been widely planted as forage for cattle because it is so hardy, withstanding grazing and trampling, and it can be made into [[hay]]. However, it is not one of the more [[palatable]] or nutritious grasses. It is also good for [[erosion]] control because it binds the soil. Indeed, it is still recommended for planting along shorelines to stabilize them.<ref name=usda>[https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/pg_pare3.pdf Torpedograss ''Panicum repens'' L.] USDA NRCS Plant Guide.</ref>
